Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

The default daemon can keep many tabs and visit many sites; browser-use has

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

    14	# Matveyev's Table 8.2: Competitive Exercises Grouped as Monostructural, Polystructural or Complexes
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors present Matveyev's "classification of competitive exercises" as a further illustration of "the meticulous attention to detail used in the Russian system" (PDF 445 / p.434). Table 8.2, "Categorisation of Competitive Exercises in Different Types of Sport," read from the page image, has three overall groupings:
    17	- *Monostructural Exercises (relatively stable forms)*: 1. Speed and Strength Exercises (A. Jumps; B. Throws (Shot, javelin, etc); C. Lifting weights; D. Sprint); 2. Cyclic Endurance (A. High intensity endurance events; B. Low and medium intensity endurance).
    18	- *Polystructural Exercises (variable forms)*: 1. Team Games (A. High intensity interval; B. Prolonged relatively continuous); 2. Sporting Combat (A. Non physical contact (fencing etc); B. Physical Contact (boxing, wrestling etc)).
    19	- *Complexes of Exercises*: 1. Dual and Combined Events with a stable content (A. Homogeneous Two-event & Combined events (skating 4-events, Alpine 3-events etc); B. Non-homogeneous dual and combined events (decathlon, pentathlon, ski dual etc)); 2. Dual and Combined Events with a periodically renewed content (A. Aesthetic Sports (gymnastics, diving, skating, acrobatics etc)).
    20	
    21	**Why it works** — The book gives the table without a stated rationale. Inference: the top split is by how stable the movement form is (fixed versus variable versus a set of events), and the second split is by the dominant quality or contact demand, which are the features that decide how specific the special preparatory work can be.
    22	
    23	**When to apply** — As a first sort when a coach meets an unfamiliar sport: place it in a cell, then borrow programming from neighbours in that cell. Inference: American football sits under Polystructural, Team Games, A (high intensity interval), the same cell as other field sports with repeated short efforts.
    24	
    25	**When NOT to apply** — The table carries no data and no stated purpose beyond illustration. Some cells are thin: Dual and Combined Events "with a periodically renewed content" has a single subgroup, aesthetic sports. Skating appears both in the homogeneous combined events and among aesthetic sports, so a sport can fall in more than one cell. The 6.7 classification by Farfel (acyclic, cyclic, complex) cuts the same sports differently, by movement organisation and energy supply (see [[framework--three-sport-groups-acyclic-cyclic-complex-for-programming]]); the two schemes are different lenses, not a conflict. Note the book reuses the label "Table 8.2" on PDF 453 / p.442 for the A/B overtraining comparison, which is printed as Table 8.3 on PDF 454.
    26	
    27	**Example** — The table's own placements: sprint and weightlifting are monostructural speed-strength exercises, while boxing and wrestling are polystructural combat with physical contact (PDF 445 / p.434, checked against the page image).

    14	# Medvedev's Weightlifting Classification: Competition, Special Preparatory and General Groups, Recast as 12 Fundamental and 4 Additional Means
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors offer the Russian weightlifting scheme as a model that "may then be applied in any other sport" (PDF 445 / p.434). Per Medvedev (1986): "Group 1 consists of the competition exercises (in weightlifting, the Snatch and Clean & Jerk)"; "Group 2 combines the Special Preparatory exercises," subdivided into auxiliary snatch exercises, auxiliary clean and jerk exercises, and "auxiliary exercises for the legs, back, (torso), arms and shoulder girdle"; "Group 3 consists of General Preparatory exercises" (PDF 445, checked against the page image). The passage that follows, presented under Medvedev's classification, then regroups them by effect. Group 1 "combines the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means," mostly "in conformity with the technique of the classic Snatch and classic Clean & Jerk," lifted heavy "at great power," so it is "the fundamental group." Group 2 holds the "special preparatory (developmental) exercises," which "for the most part ... have a local effect," use "relatively light weights," develop "relatively small" power and "can be significantly different in technique" (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). "The fundamental exercises are divided into 12 groups and the additional exercises into 4 groups" (PDF 446 / p.435): fundamental 1-12 are classic snatch, squat snatch, power snatch, snatch pull, classic clean and jerk, squat clean, jerk, power clean, clean pull, barbell squats, good mornings and pressing; additional 13-16 are leg exercises, back exercises, arm and shoulder girdle exercises, and "The Snatch and Clean & Jerk Exercises with weights less than 60%" (PDF 446, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The stated reason for the regrouping: all exercises, "depending on their coordination structure, method of training and amount of resistance," develop physical qualities and contribute to "the perfecting of technical mastery" to different extents, so "it is appropriate to divide all of the exercises of the first and second groups into two independent parts" (PDF 445 / p.434). Inference: the split sorts exercises by the size of the training effect they carry, so that heavy, technique-matched lifting can be tracked apart from light local work.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When building a classification for a sport's own exercise pool, use the two passes the book models: first by resemblance (competition, special, general), then by effect (fundamental versus additional). Inference: the clean, jerk and squat variants Eric names as core work (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104) would sit in the fundamental group; single-joint assistance work would be additional.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The scheme is weightlifting-specific and the book reports no outcome data for it. The source is internally loose: Group 1 is first "the competition exercises" and then "the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means" (PDF 445), and the light snatch and clean and jerk under 60% move to the additional group. The numbered list of "One hundred different weightlifting exercises" that follows (PDF 447-449 / p.436-438) uses its own group numbering, which jumps from Group 7 to Group 9 with no Group 8 heading (PDF 448 / p.437), and has no entry for the under-60% group. The 100-exercise list itself is not atomized here.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Pull variants show how one fundamental group expands in the 100-exercise list: snatch pulls from the floor, from below, at and above the knee, from a block, "with four, 3-second stops (at the instant of starting lift, at knees, above the knees, heels raised)," slow then fast, and combined with the full snatch (items 15-28, PDF 447-448 / p.436-437, checked against the page images).

    14	# Count Fundamental and Additional Training Loads Separately, Not as One Total
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In the weightlifting classification the book presents under Medvedev (1986): "in order to more objectively assess the training influence, the athlete is subjected to exercises from Group 1, their loading is counted as fundamental, while the loading in the Group 2 is considered additional. Finally, it is important that *fundamental and additional training loads should be calculated and analysed separately*" (PDF 446 / p.435, italics in the original, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The passage's reasoning: Group 1 lifts are heavy, close to competition technique and done "at great power," while Group 2 lifts are light, local and develop "relatively small" power (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). Inference: one tonnage total would let a large volume of light local work mask a drop in heavy competition-pattern work, or the reverse, so the two need separate columns to show what the athlete actually did.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — In any training log that sums volume (lifts, tonnage, reps above a percentage), keep at least two totals: the core lifts that carry the main training effect, and the assistance work. Separating totals does not say how to weight them against each other.

# Matveyev's Table 8.2: Competitive Exercises Grouped as Monostructural, Polystructural or Complexes

**What it is** — The authors present Matveyev's "classification of competitive exercises" as a further illustration of "the meticulous attention to detail used in the Russian system" (PDF 445 / p.434). Table 8.2, "Categorisation of Competitive Exercises in Different Types of Sport," read from the page image, has three overall groupings:
- *Monostructural Exercises (relatively stable forms)*: 1. Speed and Strength Exercises (A. Jumps; B. Throws (Shot, javelin, etc); C. Lifting weights; D. Sprint); 2. Cyclic Endurance (A. High intensity endurance events; B. Low and medium intensity endurance).
- *Polystructural Exercises (variable forms)*: 1. Team Games (A. High intensity interval; B. Prolonged relatively continuous); 2. Sporting Combat (A. Non physical contact (fencing etc); B. Physical Contact (boxing, wrestling etc)).
- *Complexes of Exercises*: 1. Dual and Combined Events with a stable content (A. Homogeneous Two-event & Combined events (skating 4-events, Alpine 3-events etc); B. Non-homogeneous dual and combined events (decathlon, pentathlon, ski dual etc)); 2. Dual and Combined Events with a periodically renewed content (A. Aesthetic Sports (gymnastics, diving, skating, acrobatics etc)).

**Why it works** — The book gives the table without a stated rationale. Inference: the top split is by how stable the movement form is (fixed versus variable versus a set of events), and the second split is by the dominant quality or contact demand, which are the features that decide how specific the special preparatory work can be.

**When to apply** — As a first sort when a coach meets an unfamiliar sport: place it in a cell, then borrow programming from neighbours in that cell. Inference: American football sits under Polystructural, Team Games, A (high intensity interval), the same cell as other field sports with repeated short efforts.

**When NOT to apply** — The table carries no data and no stated purpose beyond illustration. Some cells are thin: Dual and Combined Events "with a periodically renewed content" has a single subgroup, aesthetic sports. Skating appears both in the homogeneous combined events and among aesthetic sports, so a sport can fall in more than one cell. The 6.7 classification by Farfel (acyclic, cyclic, complex) cuts the same sports differently, by movement organisation and energy supply (see [[framework--three-sport-groups-acyclic-cyclic-complex-for-programming]]); the two schemes are different lenses, not a conflict. Note the book reuses the label "Table 8.2" on PDF 453 / p.442 for the A/B overtraining comparison, which is printed as Table 8.3 on PDF 454.

**Example** — The table's own placements: sprint and weightlifting are monostructural speed-strength exercises, while boxing and wrestling are polystructural combat with physical contact (PDF 445 / p.434, checked against the page image).

**Related** — [[framework--competition-special-preparatory-and-general-preparatory-exercise-classes]], [[framework--three-sport-groups-acyclic-cyclic-complex-for-programming]], [[framework--eight-types-of-needs-analysis]]

# Medvedev's Weightlifting Classification: Competition, Special Preparatory and General Groups, Recast as 12 Fundamental and 4 Additional Means

**What it is** — The authors offer the Russian weightlifting scheme as a model that "may then be applied in any other sport" (PDF 445 / p.434). Per Medvedev (1986): "Group 1 consists of the competition exercises (in weightlifting, the Snatch and Clean & Jerk)"; "Group 2 combines the Special Preparatory exercises," subdivided into auxiliary snatch exercises, auxiliary clean and jerk exercises, and "auxiliary exercises for the legs, back, (torso), arms and shoulder girdle"; "Group 3 consists of General Preparatory exercises" (PDF 445, checked against the page image). The passage that follows, presented under Medvedev's classification, then regroups them by effect. Group 1 "combines the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means," mostly "in conformity with the technique of the classic Snatch and classic Clean & Jerk," lifted heavy "at great power," so it is "the fundamental group." Group 2 holds the "special preparatory (developmental) exercises," which "for the most part ... have a local effect," use "relatively light weights," develop "relatively small" power and "can be significantly different in technique" (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). "The fundamental exercises are divided into 12 groups and the additional exercises into 4 groups" (PDF 446 / p.435): fundamental 1-12 are classic snatch, squat snatch, power snatch, snatch pull, classic clean and jerk, squat clean, jerk, power clean, clean pull, barbell squats, good mornings and pressing; additional 13-16 are leg exercises, back exercises, arm and shoulder girdle exercises, and "The Snatch and Clean & Jerk Exercises with weights less than 60%" (PDF 446, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The stated reason for the regrouping: all exercises, "depending on their coordination structure, method of training and amount of resistance," develop physical qualities and contribute to "the perfecting of technical mastery" to different extents, so "it is appropriate to divide all of the exercises of the first and second groups into two independent parts" (PDF 445 / p.434). Inference: the split sorts exercises by the size of the training effect they carry, so that heavy, technique-matched lifting can be tracked apart from light local work.

**When to apply** — When building a classification for a sport's own exercise pool, use the two passes the book models: first by resemblance (competition, special, general), then by effect (fundamental versus additional). Inference: the clean, jerk and squat variants Eric names as core work (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104) would sit in the fundamental group; single-joint assistance work would be additional.

**When NOT to apply** — The scheme is weightlifting-specific and the book reports no outcome data for it. The source is internally loose: Group 1 is first "the competition exercises" and then "the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means" (PDF 445), and the light snatch and clean and jerk under 60% move to the additional group. The numbered list of "One hundred different weightlifting exercises" that follows (PDF 447-449 / p.436-438) uses its own group numbering, which jumps from Group 7 to Group 9 with no Group 8 heading (PDF 448 / p.437), and has no entry for the under-60% group. The 100-exercise list itself is not atomized here.

**Example** — Pull variants show how one fundamental group expands in the 100-exercise list: snatch pulls from the floor, from below, at and above the knee, from a block, "with four, 3-second stops (at the instant of starting lift, at knees, above the knees, heels raised)," slow then fast, and combined with the full snatch (items 15-28, PDF 447-448 / p.436-437, checked against the page images).

**Related** — [[framework--competition-special-preparatory-and-general-preparatory-exercise-classes]], [[heuristic--calculate-fundamental-and-additional-training-loads-separately]], [[principle--high-volume-wide-range-assistance-work-lets-tendons-keep-pace-with-speed-strength]], [[heuristic--general-preparatory-exercises-three-functions-and-two-selection-rules]], [[case-study--vorobyev-ermakov-weightlifting-load-distributions]], [[framework--bench-squat-and-deadlift-variation-axes]]

# Count Fundamental and Additional Training Loads Separately, Not as One Total

**What it is** — In the weightlifting classification the book presents under Medvedev (1986): "in order to more objectively assess the training influence, the athlete is subjected to exercises from Group 1, their loading is counted as fundamental, while the loading in the Group 2 is considered additional. Finally, it is important that *fundamental and additional training loads should be calculated and analysed separately*" (PDF 446 / p.435, italics in the original, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The passage's reasoning: Group 1 lifts are heavy, close to competition technique and done "at great power," while Group 2 lifts are light, local and develop "relatively small" power (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). Inference: one tonnage total would let a large volume of light local work mask a drop in heavy competition-pattern work, or the reverse, so the two need separate columns to show what the athlete actually did.

**When to apply** — In any training log that sums volume (lifts, tonnage, reps above a percentage), keep at least two totals: the core lifts that carry the main training effect, and the assistance work. Inference: in a team setting this is the line between the multi-joint lifts Eric weights training time toward and the "small share" of single-joint work (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)).

**When NOT to apply** — The rule is stated, not tested; the book gives no example of a decision that changed because the two totals were separated. The fundamental/additional line is drawn for weightlifting; Inference: in other sports the line has to be redrawn from that sport's own classification. Separating totals does not say how to weight them against each other.

**Example** — Inference, using the 16-group scheme on PDF 446: a week with 120 lifts above 70% in snatch, clean and jerk, pulls and squats (fundamental groups 1-12) and 200 reps of lunges, good mornings and presses (additional groups 13-15) is logged as two numbers, not as 320 reps.

**Related** — [[framework--medvedev-weightlifting-exercise-groups-fundamental-and-additional-means]], [[framework--volume-intensity-and-relative-intensity-calculation]], [[case-study--vorobyev-ermakov-weightlifting-load-distributions]], [[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]]

# Count Fundamental and Additional Training Loads Separately, Not as One Total

**What it is** — In the weightlifting classification the book presents under Medvedev (1986): "in order to more objectively assess the training influence, the athlete is subjected to exercises from Group 1, their loading is counted as fundamental, while the loading in the Group 2 is considered additional. Finally, it is important that *fundamental and additional training loads should be calculated and analysed separately*" (PDF 446 / p.435, italics in the original, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The passage's reasoning: Group 1 lifts are heavy, close to competition technique and done "at great power," while Group 2 lifts are light, local and develop "relatively small" power (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). Inference: one tonnage total would let a large volume of light local work mask a drop in heavy competition-pattern work, or the reverse, so the two need separate columns to show what the athlete actually did.

**When to apply** — In any training log that sums volume (lifts, tonnage, reps above a percentage), keep at least two totals: the core lifts that carry the main training effect, and the assistance work. Inference: in a team setting the line falls between heavy, high-power lifts in the competition pattern and lighter, local work that differs in technique, not between multi-joint and single-joint lifts; many of the multi-joint lifts Eric weights training time toward (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)) would land on the additional side.

**When NOT to apply** — The rule is stated, not tested; the book gives no example of a decision that changed because the two totals were separated. The fundamental/additional line is drawn for weightlifting; Inference: in other sports the line has to be redrawn from that sport's own classification. Separating totals does not say how to weight them against each other.

**Example** — Inference, using the 16-group scheme on PDF 446: a week with 120 lifts above 70% in snatch, clean and jerk, pulls and squats (fundamental groups 1-12) and 200 reps of lunges, good mornings and presses (additional groups 13-15) is logged as two numbers, not as 320 reps.

# Two Types of General Overtraining: A (Addisonic, Parasympathetic, Quiet) and B (Basedowic, Sympathetic, Obvious), Table 8.3

**What it is** — The authors tie general overtraining to the endocrine system. Fig 8.3 ("Some of the physiological control systems involved with motor processes") draws the hypothalamus linked to the central nervous system ("Fast Control") and the endocrine system ("Slow Control"), both linked to the muscular system (PDF 453 / p.442, read from the figure). Since hormones are central to stress, "it is logical to associate general overtraining, a stress related phenomenon, with some disturbance of the endocrine system," and "Researchers sometimes identify at least two types of general overtraining on this basis (Israel, 1963)" (PDF 453). *A-overtraining* (Addisonic), after Addison's disease ("diminished activity of the adrenal glands"), "affects predominantly the parasympathetic pathways" and "is difficult to detect early, due to the absence of any dramatic symptoms"; stagnation or deterioration of performance may be the first clue. *B-overtraining* (Basedowic), after Basedow's disease ("thyroid hyperactivity"), "affects predominantly the sympathetic pathways" and, "as the classical type of overtraining with its abundance of symptoms, is easy to diagnose" (PDF 453 / p.442, checked against the page image). Table 8.3, "Symptomatic comparison of A and B types of overtraining" (PDF 454 / p.443, read from the page image), A then B:
1. Blood pressure: "diastolic increase to over 100mm Hg, during and after physical stress" / "slight increase"
2. Coordination: impaired / "impaired, with increased reaction time"
3. Bodymass: normal / decrease
4. Endurance: "slight increase in tiredness" / "tendency to tire easily"
5. Sleep requirements: "no increase" / increase
6. Resting pulse: low / elevated
7. Body temperature: normal / "slightly increased"
8. Appetite: normal / reduced
9. Metabolism: normal / "altered, with increased tendency to sweat: abnormally increased breathing rate under stress"
10. General muscle soreness: "little or none" / "mild to pronounced, with tendency to muscle stiffness and pain"
11. General resistance: normal / "tendency to headaches, colds, fever blisters; prolonged recuperation"
12. Recovery time: "normal or slightly increased" / increased
13. Psychological changes: "none, other than slight loss in motivation" / "nervousness, poor motivation, inner unease, eventual depression"
The authors add that overtraining "has also been shown to be associated with electrocardiographic changes, in particular a smaller T wave," so the table "could no doubt be extended" (PDF 454).

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale is the endocrine link: the adrenals "selectively prepare the skeletal muscle for physical activity in the face of stress," thyroxine raises the rate cells burn fuel and joins "anti-stress responses" (PDF 453). Inference: the two pictures follow the autonomic direction, so B shows raised drive (pulse, temperature, sweating, nervousness) and A shows damped drive with few signs.

**When to apply** — As a reminder that a quiet athlete can be overtrained. Inference: a low resting pulse with stalled performance and no complaints fits the A picture, which the authors say is "difficult to detect early"; a performance check is then the main signal.

**When NOT to apply** — The table carries one citation (Israel, 1963) and no data, thresholds or sample; `untested`. The text on PDF 453 says the types "are compared in Table 8.2," but the table on PDF 454 is printed as Table 8.3; Table 8.2 is Matveyev's sport classification on PDF 445. Two library sources split overtraining the same way but differ in detail: Samuels lists low resting blood pressure for the parasympathetic type, while Table 8.3 gives an A-type diastolic rise "during and after physical stress," a different measurement condition, not the same claim. Samuels has disturbed sleep in the sympathetic type and none in the parasympathetic, and Table 8.3 has increased sleep requirement only in B; these align. Not marked `contested`. Inference: naming the types after Addison's and Basedow's diseases is an analogy; the book does not claim athletes have those diseases.

**Example** — The authors' own contrast: the B type, "the classical type of overtraining with its abundance of symptoms, is easy to diagnose," while for the A type, "Suspicion that something is amiss may be aroused by the appearance of stagnation or deterioration of the athlete's performance" (PDF 453 / p.442).

**Related** — [[overtraining-and-sleep--samuels/framework--sympathetic-and-parasympathetic-overtraining-signs]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]], [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic]], [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]]

# Restoration Is Planned Into Training and Is Not Rehabilitation; Most Rehabilitation Follows Failed Pedagogical Restoration

**What it is** — The authors open 8.6: "Restoration is an integral part of overall training and practice, so that it must be applied with the short-term and long-term goals constantly in mind. A comprehensive training programme alternates different training techniques with situationally appropriate restorative means." The distinction: "*restoration* in training and competition is not synonymous with *rehabilitation*, which refers to the treatment of overtraining, illness or injury" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). They return to it on the next page: "Restoration is an integral part of the overall training programme, planned to fit in at the most effective and appropriate stages of training. Rehabilitation refers to therapy to restore an injured athlete to full functional capability. Very often the need for rehabilitation is the consequence of inadequate restoration, especially imperfect pedagogical restoration, i.e. a training schedule which produces overtraining" (PDF 456 / p.445, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' causal claim is in the last sentence: a schedule that overtrains creates the injuries that then need rehabilitation. "Although accidents can happen which are largely outside the control of the athlete, the essence of training is to maximise performance and minimise injuries, pain and soreness" (PDF 456). Inference: on this view, restoration is a planning job owned by whoever writes the training, while rehabilitation is a treatment job, so a rise in rehab caseload is first a question about the programme.

**When to apply** — When rehab cases cluster, audit the training schedule ("pedagogical restoration") before adding treatments. When planning, put restoration in the plan at set stages rather than leaving it to the athlete's request. Eric's review: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: Eric's load-design approach is what the authors call pedagogical restoration; the book's other two classes (medico-biological and psychological, see [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]]) have no counterpart in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — "Very often" is not quantified and no injury data are given. The authors also say "Full restoration can sometimes be undesirable" and that "some Russian experts emphasize the importance of periodically training on a basis of *non-recovery* (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 455), so integral restoration does not mean full recovery between every session (see [[heuristic--incomplete-restoration-workouts-zalessky-rules]]). Accidents fall outside the claim by the authors' own words.

**Example** — The authors' description of top Russian practice: "It is not unusual for top Russian athletes to receive over an hour of restoration every day, with regular alternation of individualised methods and periodic training superimposed on a state of non-restoration" (PDF 456 / p.445).

**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]], [[principle--return-to-play-incomplete-until-the-athlete-perceives-full-healing]], [[heuristic--six-strength-training-causes-of-overtraining-injury]], [[principle--periodise-restoration-in-complexes-not-at-random]]

# Medvedev's Weightlifting Classification: Competition, Special Preparatory and General Groups, Recast as 12 Fundamental and 4 Additional Means

**What it is** — The authors offer the Russian weightlifting scheme as a model that "may then be applied in any other sport" (PDF 445 / p.434). Per Medvedev (1986): "Group 1 consists of the competition exercises (in weightlifting, the Snatch and Clean & Jerk)"; "Group 2 combines the Special Preparatory exercises," subdivided into auxiliary snatch exercises, auxiliary clean and jerk exercises, and "auxiliary exercises for the legs, back, (torso), arms and shoulder girdle"; "Group 3 consists of General Preparatory exercises" (PDF 445, checked against the page image). The passage that follows, presented under Medvedev's classification, then regroups them by effect. Group 1 "combines the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means," mostly "in conformity with the technique of the classic Snatch and classic Clean & Jerk," lifted heavy "at great power," so it is "the fundamental group." Group 2 holds the "special preparatory (developmental) exercises," which "for the most part ... have a local effect," use "relatively light weights," develop "relatively small" power and "can be significantly different in technique" (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). "The fundamental exercises are divided into 12 groups and the additional exercises into 4 groups" (PDF 446 / p.435): fundamental 1-12 are classic snatch, squat snatch, power snatch, snatch pull, classic clean and jerk, squat clean, jerk, power clean, clean pull, barbell squats, good mornings and pressing; additional 13-16 are leg exercises, back exercises, arm and shoulder girdle exercises, and "The Snatch and Clean & Jerk Exercises with weights less than 60%" (PDF 446, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The stated reason for the regrouping: all exercises, "depending on their coordination structure, method of training and amount of resistance," develop physical qualities and contribute to "the perfecting of technical mastery" to different extents, so "it is appropriate to divide all of the exercises of the first and second groups into two independent parts" (PDF 445 / p.434). Inference: the split sorts exercises by the size of the training effect they carry, so that heavy, technique-matched lifting can be tracked apart from light local work.

**When to apply** — When building a classification for a sport's own exercise pool, use the two passes the book models: first by resemblance (competition, special, general), then by effect (fundamental versus additional). The book's line between the two parts is conformity with competition technique and power output, not joint count: the additional groups are lunges, jumps with a barbell and leg press (13), good mornings and hyperextensions (14), rows and presses (15), and the snatch and clean and jerk under 60% (16) (PDF 446 / p.435).

**When NOT to apply** — The scheme is weightlifting-specific and the book reports no outcome data for it. The source is internally loose: Group 1 is first "the competition exercises" and then "the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means" (PDF 445), and the light snatch and clean and jerk under 60% move to the additional group. The 100-exercise list itself is not atomized here.

**Example** — Pull variants show how one fundamental group expands in the 100-exercise list: snatch pulls from the floor, from below, at and above the knee, from a block, "with four, 3-second stops (at the instant of starting lift, at knees, above the knees, heels raised)," slow then fast, and combined with the full snatch (items 15-28, PDF 447-448 / p.436-437, checked against the page images).

=== framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological.md

# Three Classes of Restoration: Pedagogical (Coaching), Medico-Biological and Psychological, Plus Natural Recovery Outside Training

**What it is** — "The Russians usually recognise three classes of restoration (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 456 / p.445, checked against the page image):
- *Pedagogical (coaching) restoration* "employs carefully periodised programmes to optimise the balance between training stresses and natural recuperative processes." It includes "combinational training, known in the West as 'cross training'," active rest, and "Low intensity cyclical, rhythmical, circulatory or cardiovascular activities" after "demanding strength training sessions." Micro-, meso- and macrocycles, with the preparatory period split into General and Special Physical Preparation, exist "specifically to promote supercompensation via suitable phasing of loading and restoration regimes (see Ch 6)."
- *Medico-biological restoration* covers "therapeutic measures offered by medical and allied practitioners," sometimes split into physiotherapeutic and pharmacological measures. Physical measures divide into natural means ("massage, showers, heat, sunlight and training outdoors") and additional means ("electrostimulation, electrosleep, diathermy, acupuncture, baro-chambers, laser therapy and ultrasound").
- *Psychological restoration* "involves management of the mental state": hypnosis, self-hypnosis, auto-suggestion, autogenics, visualisation, progressive relaxation, guided imagery, music therapy and learning techniques, some using biofeedback or electrodermal devices.
Beyond these, "it is essential to encourage natural recovery relating to family, living conditions, lifestyle, nutrition, leisure activities, beneficial socialisation, team atmosphere, work conditions, spiritual needs and coaching team interaction" (PDF 456). A later restatement (PDF 458 / p.447, read from the page image) puts pedagogical methods "outside the scope of this text" and splits the rest into physical, medical and psychological means. Table 8.5 subdivides them: physical (passive, active, combined); medical (pharmacological, psychiatric, surgical, nutritional, combined); psychological (therapist-administered, self-administered, combined). Table 8.6 lists physical means in three columns, active means mainly in the last (for example physical activity, recreational sport, manual labour, dance, play, postural realignment, breathing regimens, progressive relaxation, Tai Chi, yoga); Table 8.7 lists 14 psychological means from psychotherapy to "Laughter/tears" (PDF 459 / p.448).

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale for the system is its specificity: "The Russian restoration system recognises the *specificity of each technique or sequence of techniques* for a particular sport, phase of training, individual athlete, time of the day, type of stress and type of fitness," applied "before, during, shortly after and a long time after training and competitions," with "Meticulous records" of daily physical and psychological state (PDF 456). On natural recovery: "problems which lie outside the training setting can easily predominate over training problems in determining the success of the athlete in competition" (PDF 456).

**When to apply** — As a coverage check on a recovery plan: is there a pedagogical element (load phasing, active rest), a medico-biological element (by whom), a psychological element, and attention to life outside training? The authors also note that "the athlete is encouraged to shed dependence on the therapist and to learn *self-restoration* procedures (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 456). Eric's review: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: by the book's scheme that is the pedagogical class only.

**When NOT to apply** — The categories are descriptive; the authors say Table 8.5 "should not be regarded as definitive or exclusive" (PDF 458). The lists mix well-studied means with ones that have little support (for example "Religion," "Screaming/shouting" in Table 8.7; "Therapeutic Touch," "Aromatherapy" in Table 8.6); inclusion is not endorsement of effect. Inference: the medico-biological class includes pharmacological means; anything in that class sits with the medical staff, not the strength coach.

**Example** — The pedagogical example the authors give: "Low intensity cyclical, rhythmical, circulatory or cardiovascular activities can also be very useful for promoting recovery after demanding strength training sessions" (PDF 456 / p.445).

**Related** — [[principle--restoration-is-part-of-training-and-distinct-from-rehabilitation]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]], [[framework--restoration-prescription-checklist-and-means-versus-methods]], [[framework--methods-for-improving-voluntary-muscle-relaxation]], [[browns-strength-and-conditioning-2008--myslinski/heuristic--restoration-emphasis-rises-as-the-off-season-advances]]
=== claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect.md

# Belief and Rapport Carry Much of a Restoration Technique's Effect, Which Is Both a Tool and a Confound

**What it is** — The authors: "Certainly, many of these techniques may work because they are placebos, because the user believes in them. Yet, this is a very good reason not to dismiss them." If the mind can be focused "by an apparently illogical or foolish concept to perform unusual feats of performance or healing, then it is vital that we uncover the underlying physiological principles which make the *placebo effect* (or 'faith factor') so powerful. Placebos can produce positive and negative effects; it is up to science to sift the useful from the harmful" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). The same effect "can also confound the validity of many restoration techniques, which work not because of any special merits, but because the practitioner persuades the user of its value." Hence "Virtually every claim by one massage therapist will be countered by another 'expert'" (PDF 455). On rapport: "the therapy often succeeds because of the rapport between therapist and client," and in sports restoration "*The rapport between you and the athlete is central to the success of the therapy*. In short, the belief of the athlete in you and your therapy (and sometimes an outside force, depending on the athlete's belief system) is an integral part of successful restoration" (PDF 456 / p.445, italics in the original, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "physical and mental healing are inextricably linked," so "one cannot separate the therapy from the therapist" (PDF 456). They draw the research consequence: "great care has to be taken to choose experimental and control groups and to exclude as far as possible all confounding factors such as the placebo effect and human interaction" (PDF 456). The 8.6 closing list makes the same point as propositions: "Virtually any technique will work, irrespective of scientific validity, if you believe in it," and a technique "obtained at high cost," taught "in an exciting, emotional or challenging way," or that "appeals to the basic beliefs, prejudices and background of the user is more likely to succeed" (items 1-4, PDF 467 / p.456).

**When to apply** — Two uses. Practice: before using any restoration means, "consider the background and attitudes of the athlete, because these factors can have a profound effect on the efficacy of any regime" (PDF 458 / p.447). Evaluation: when a staff member reports that a modality works, ask whether the comparison controlled for belief and attention. Inference: Eric's account of abandoned wellness surveys, where athletes learned what answers the survey rewarded (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89), is a reminder that self-report after a treatment carries the same bias.

**When NOT to apply** — These are the authors' opinions; no placebo-controlled data are given here. Two pages later the authors push the other way: "This [sic] is sometimes a tendency to dismiss the effects of many restorative means as placebo or psychological in origin," which their Russian research summary is meant "to correct" (PDF 465 / p.454; see [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]]). The two positions are not a contradiction in the book's own terms: belief adds to some real effects, and confounds the rest. Using belief deliberately raises an honesty question the book does not address.

**Example** — The authors' own contrast: "one therapist will swear that aromatherapy with a certain fragrance will help, while another may claim the opposite. Another will extol the virtue of deep transverse friction for adhesions, whereas yet another will have equal success with therapeutic touch" (PDF 455 / p.444).

**Related** — [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]], [[framework--eighteen-propositions-on-sport-science-and-stress-management]], [[heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]]
=== framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring.md

# What Stress Changes (Table 8.4), and Why Motor Control Belongs on the Monitoring List

**What it is** — Table 8.4, "Functions affected by physiological and psychological stress," introduced as "some of the symptoms of overtraining stress" (PDF 456 / p.445), lists 20 functions in three columns (PDF 457 / p.446, read from the page image): heart rate; blood pressure; muscular tension; muscle irritability; pain threshold; brain rhythms; breathing patterns; sleep patterns; body temperature; concentration and alertness; digestion, gastric acidity; endocrine secretion; immune response; fine motor control; reaction time; posture; pupil size (of the eye); general irritability, mood, stability; tissue repair and growth; secretion of endogenous opiates. The authors: "stress produces acute (short-term) and chronic (long-term) effects on variables including those listed in Table 8.4. There are many standard tests for and ways of observing most of the indicators of stress below; the thorough preparation of the athlete demands that they be applied regularly and appropriate restoration interventions be used" (PDF 457). Later they single out motor control: "careful attention has to be paid to changes in motor control or movement skill, since all sporting action relies fundamentally on muscle action controlled by the nervous system," which is why they earlier recommended "the coach making regular ratings of the technical perfection of the athlete's execution of important movements." "Quantitative measurement of individual indicators of motor proficiency, such as balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills, can also furnish useful data" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for motor control: it applies even to "training which does not necessarily place great demands on qualities such as strength and endurance" (PDF 461), because all sporting action runs through the nervous system. Inference: a technique or coordination drop can show stress in skill-dominant athletes before strength or endurance tests move.

**When to apply** — When choosing what to monitor, pick a few Table 8.4 functions that have a cheap test, and add one motor-control measure or a coach rating of technique. Eric's review: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: mRSI is a neuromuscular output measure; the book's list suggests reaction time or a coach technique rating as the complementary motor-control read.

**When NOT to apply** — The table is a list of functions, not a validated battery; it gives no tests, norms or thresholds, and "applied regularly" is not defined. Several items (brain rhythms, endogenous opiates, pupil size) need laboratory access. The authors' own text slips: it calls the table "symptoms of overtraining stress" and also functions affected by stress in general.

**Example** — The authors' motor-control battery: "balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills" (PDF 461 / p.450).

**Related** — [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]], [[framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3]], [[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]], [[case-study--makarova-stupnitsky-weekly-four-group-restoration-triage-fig-8-4]], [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]
=== case-study--makarova-stupnitsky-weekly-four-group-restoration-triage-fig-8-4.md

# Makarova and Stupnitsky: Weekly Neuromuscular Screening Sorted Athletes Into Four Groups, Each With Its Own Restoration (Fig 8.4)

**What it is** — The authors describe a year-long applied system (Makarova & Stupnitsky, 1983). For athletes with access to scientific institutes, neuromuscular system (NMS) state "may be assessed by methods such as monitoring of the quasi-stationary electrical potential of the brain, quantitative muscle palpation (using probes such as the myotonometer devised by Siff) and measurement of skin conductance or impedance at acupuncture points (Shishkin, 1989)." Makarova & Stupnitsky found that local muscle contraction (LMC) measured by tonometry "displays a clear topography and often coincides with the acupuncture points," and that "pronounced LMC" coincided "with a poorer functional state of the NMS," together with "increased muscle tonus, decreased strength, an increase in time for muscle relaxation and impaired rheographic indicators" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image). Over year-long programmes they saw "a characteristic change in the skin impedance whenever there is significant disruption in the athlete's adaptation," and used it, "sometimes assisted by other standard physiological tests (such as heart rate, blood pressure, flicker fusion rate in vision and reaction time)," to adjust training and restoration (PDF 461). Athletes were sorted by these indicators and their self-perception: Group I, "no disruptions in self-feeling, work capacity or NMS"; Group II, "minor local disturbances"; Group III, "definite complaints and muscle disturbances"; Group IV, "acute illnesses (colds etc.)" (PDF 461). "This diagnostic process was repeated once per weekly microcycle." Restoration went mainly to Groups II-IV, "with minimal application to those in Group I." Group II received "point-reflexive and local reflexive procedures focusing on the problematic body zones," with "a small amount of general restoration"; in Group IV "general restoration means predominated over lesser used local reflexive methods," with the rehabilitative process "under medical supervision" (PDF 461-462 / p.450-451). Fig 8.4, "Organisation of the systems of restoration for athletes," read from the figure as far as its arrows can be traced (PDF 462 / p.451): Evaluation of the Functional State, linked to Consideration of Current Condition, feeds Groups I-IV; Groups II-IV feed Restorative Procedures, with an arrow from the groups to Therapeutic Procedures; Group I and Restorative Procedures feed the Training Process, which loops back to evaluation.

**Why it works** — The authors' account: these indicators "point to a diminished work capacity" (PDF 461), so they can direct restoration to the athletes who need it and leave the rest alone. Inference: it is a triage system; Group I athletes get almost no restoration, consistent with the book's warning that routine restoration can blunt adaptation.

**When to apply** — As a model for weekly triage: one screen per microcycle, a simple four-way sort (fine; local issue; general complaint; ill), and a different response for each, rather than one recovery routine for the roster.

**When NOT to apply** — The book reports the design, not the outcomes; no numbers, sample size or comparison group are given, so `supported` rests only on a named, year-long applied study described in some detail. The measures (skin impedance at acupuncture points, quasi-stationary brain potential) are specialist and not standard practice. The text on PDF 461 refers the four groups to "(Fig 8.3)," but Fig 8.3 is the control-systems diagram on PDF 453; the restoration figure is Fig 8.4 on PDF 462. The text says Group II falls "between Groups I and III" while the group numbers suggest severity rises to IV; Group IV is illness, a different kind of state.

**Example** — The weekly sort as the authors give it: Group II gets local reflexive procedures on the problem zones plus a little general restoration; Group IV gets mainly general restoration under medical supervision (PDF 462 / p.451).

**Related** — [[framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring]], [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]], [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]]
=== heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads.md

# Judge a Restoration Method by Performance and Injuries, Not Client Feeling, and Test It Under Sport-Typical Loads

**What it is** — Two rules for evaluating restoration. First: "Client feeling and appreciation are not enough; in sports restoration, the basic indicators are improved performance and fewer injuries." The reader should "experiment with variations, to keep records and to devise recipes which consistently yield successful results" (PDF 460 / p.449, checked against the page image). Second, from Talyshev (1977): because "it is very difficult to evaluate the effectiveness of specific recovery method," it "is more advisable to test the effectiveness of a specific recovery method by using test loads that approximate most closely the natural training conditions, by using loads in sports exercises that are typically encountered in a given sport" (PDF 460-461 / p.449-450, checked against the page images).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for caution: "if certain recovery methods are employed after a workout, then the positive after-effects (or training effect) stimulated by the workout tend to be negated," so "the unskilled use of recovery methods can markedly increase the amount of training work and yet not provide a corresponding training effect" (PDF 460 / p.449). Inference: an athlete can feel better and train more while adapting less, so feeling and session volume are the wrong outcome measures; performance and injury rate capture the net effect.

**When to apply** — When a modality is adopted or kept, write down what outcome it is meant to change, track performance and injuries across its use, and test it with the sport's own loads (for example a repeated-sprint or practice-like session) rather than a lab task. Eric's review: "Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89, Explicit). Inference: the same distrust of self-report that ended the surveys applies to "this feels good" as evidence for a recovery tool.

**When NOT to apply** — Performance and injury rate are slow, noisy outcomes; Inference: with a small group they cannot separate one modality's effect within a season, so the rule supports keeping records over time rather than quick verdicts. The book gives no example of a method that was dropped under this rule. Feeling still matters for adherence and is part of the placebo effect the authors elsewhere call useful (see [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]]).

**Example** — The authors' framing of Russian work: "systematic use of recovery methods makes it possible to significantly and sometimes rapidly increase the volume and intensity of training while simultaneously decreasing the incidence of musculoskeletal injuries" (PDF 460 / p.449), which names the two outcomes, training capacity and injuries, they want restoration judged on.

**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]], [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]], [[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]]

**Example** — The pedagogical example the authors give: "Low intensity cyclical, rhythmical, circulatory or cardiovascular activities can also be very useful for promoting recovery after demanding strength training sessions" (PDF 456 / p.445).

# Belief and Rapport Carry Much of a Restoration Technique's Effect, Which Is Both a Tool and a Confound

**What it is** — The authors: "Certainly, many of these techniques may work because they are placebos, because the user believes in them. Yet, this is a very good reason not to dismiss them." If the mind can be focused "by an apparently illogical or foolish concept to perform unusual feats of performance or healing, then it is vital that we uncover the underlying physiological principles which make the *placebo effect* (or 'faith factor') so powerful. Placebos can produce positive and negative effects; it is up to science to sift the useful from the harmful" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). The same effect "can also confound the validity of many restoration techniques, which work not because of any special merits, but because the practitioner persuades the user of its value." Hence "Virtually every claim by one massage therapist will be countered by another 'expert'" (PDF 455). On rapport: "the therapy often succeeds because of the rapport between therapist and client," and in sports restoration "*The rapport between you and the athlete is central to the success of the therapy*. In short, the belief of the athlete in you and your therapy (and sometimes an outside force, depending on the athlete's belief system) is an integral part of successful restoration" (PDF 456 / p.445, italics in the original, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "physical and mental healing are inextricably linked," so "one cannot separate the therapy from the therapist" (PDF 456). They draw the research consequence: "great care has to be taken to choose experimental and control groups and to exclude as far as possible all confounding factors such as the placebo effect and human interaction" (PDF 456). The 8.6 closing list makes the same point as propositions: "Virtually any technique will work, irrespective of scientific validity, if you believe in it," and a technique "obtained at high cost," taught "in an exciting, emotional or challenging way," or that "appeals to the basic beliefs, prejudices and background of the user is more likely to succeed" (items 1-4, PDF 467 / p.456).

**When to apply** — Two uses. Practice: before using any restoration means, "consider the background and attitudes of the athlete, because these factors can have a profound effect on the efficacy of any regime" (PDF 458 / p.447). Evaluation: when a staff member reports that a modality works, ask whether the comparison controlled for belief and attention. Inference: Eric's account of abandoned wellness surveys, where athletes learned what answers the survey rewarded (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89), is a reminder that self-report after a treatment carries the same bias.

**When NOT to apply** — These are the authors' opinions; no placebo-controlled data are given here. Two pages later the authors push the other way: "This [sic] is sometimes a tendency to dismiss the effects of many restorative means as placebo or psychological in origin," which their Russian research summary is meant "to correct" (PDF 465 / p.454; see [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]]). The two positions are not a contradiction in the book's own terms: belief adds to some real effects, and confounds the rest. Using belief deliberately raises an honesty question the book does not address.

**Example** — The authors' own contrast: "one therapist will swear that aromatherapy with a certain fragrance will help, while another may claim the opposite. Another will extol the virtue of deep transverse friction for adhesions, whereas yet another will have equal success with therapeutic touch" (PDF 455 / p.444).

**Related** — [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]], [[framework--eighteen-propositions-on-sport-science-and-stress-management]], [[heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]]

# What Stress Changes (Table 8.4), and Why Motor Control Belongs on the Monitoring List

**What it is** — Table 8.4, "Functions affected by physiological and psychological stress," introduced as "some of the symptoms of overtraining stress" (PDF 456 / p.445), lists 20 functions in three columns (PDF 457 / p.446, read from the page image): heart rate; blood pressure; muscular tension; muscle irritability; pain threshold; brain rhythms; breathing patterns; sleep patterns; body temperature; concentration and alertness; digestion, gastric acidity; endocrine secretion; immune response; fine motor control; reaction time; posture; pupil size (of the eye); general irritability, mood, stability; tissue repair and growth; secretion of endogenous opiates. The authors: "stress produces acute (short-term) and chronic (long-term) effects on variables including those listed in Table 8.4. There are many standard tests for and ways of observing most of the indicators of stress below; the thorough preparation of the athlete demands that they be applied regularly and appropriate restoration interventions be used" (PDF 457). Later they single out motor control: "careful attention has to be paid to changes in motor control or movement skill, since all sporting action relies fundamentally on muscle action controlled by the nervous system," which is why they earlier recommended "the coach making regular ratings of the technical perfection of the athlete's execution of important movements." "Quantitative measurement of individual indicators of motor proficiency, such as balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills, can also furnish useful data" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for motor control: it applies even to "training which does not necessarily place great demands on qualities such as strength and endurance" (PDF 461), because all sporting action runs through the nervous system. Inference: a technique or coordination drop can show stress in skill-dominant athletes before strength or endurance tests move.

**When to apply** — When choosing what to monitor, pick a few Table 8.4 functions that have a cheap test, and add one motor-control measure or a coach rating of technique. Eric's review: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: mRSI is a neuromuscular output measure; the book's list suggests reaction time or a coach technique rating as the complementary motor-control read.

**When NOT to apply** — The table is a list of functions, not a validated battery; it gives no tests, norms or thresholds, and "applied regularly" is not defined. Several items (brain rhythms, endogenous opiates, pupil size) need laboratory access. The authors' own text slips: it calls the table "symptoms of overtraining stress" and also functions affected by stress in general.

**Example** — The authors' motor-control battery: "balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills" (PDF 461 / p.450).

# Makarova and Stupnitsky: Weekly Neuromuscular Screening Sorted Athletes Into Four Groups, Each With Its Own Restoration (Fig 8.4)

**What it is** — The authors describe a year-long applied system (Makarova & Stupnitsky, 1983). For athletes with access to scientific institutes, neuromuscular system (NMS) state "may be assessed by methods such as monitoring of the quasi-stationary electrical potential of the brain, quantitative muscle palpation (using probes such as the myotonometer devised by Siff) and measurement of skin conductance or impedance at acupuncture points (Shishkin, 1989)." Makarova & Stupnitsky found that local muscle contraction (LMC) measured by tonometry "displays a clear topography and often coincides with the acupuncture points," and that "pronounced LMC" coincided "with a poorer functional state of the NMS," together with "increased muscle tonus, decreased strength, an increase in time for muscle relaxation and impaired rheographic indicators" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image). Over year-long programmes they saw "a characteristic change in the skin impedance whenever there is significant disruption in the athlete's adaptation," and used it, "sometimes assisted by other standard physiological tests (such as heart rate, blood pressure, flicker fusion rate in vision and reaction time)," to adjust training and restoration (PDF 461). Athletes were sorted by these indicators and their self-perception: Group I, "no disruptions in self-feeling, work capacity or NMS"; Group II, "minor local disturbances"; Group III, "definite complaints and muscle disturbances"; Group IV, "acute illnesses (colds etc.)" (PDF 461). "This diagnostic process was repeated once per weekly microcycle." Restoration went mainly to Groups II-IV, "with minimal application to those in Group I." Group II received "point-reflexive and local reflexive procedures focusing on the problematic body zones," with "a small amount of general restoration"; in Group IV "general restoration means predominated over lesser used local reflexive methods," with the rehabilitative process "under medical supervision" (PDF 461-462 / p.450-451). Fig 8.4, "Organisation of the systems of restoration for athletes," read from the figure as far as its arrows can be traced (PDF 462 / p.451): Evaluation of the Functional State, linked to Consideration of Current Condition, feeds Groups I-IV; Groups II-IV feed Restorative Procedures, with an arrow from the groups to Therapeutic Procedures; Group I and Restorative Procedures feed the Training Process, which loops back to evaluation.

**Why it works** — The authors' account: these indicators "point to a diminished work capacity" (PDF 461), so they can direct restoration to the athletes who need it and leave the rest alone. Inference: it is a triage system; Group I athletes get almost no restoration, consistent with the book's warning that routine restoration can blunt adaptation.

**When to apply** — As a model for weekly triage: one screen per microcycle, a simple four-way sort (fine; local issue; general complaint; ill), and a different response for each, rather than one recovery routine for the roster.

**When NOT to apply** — The book reports the design, not the outcomes; no numbers, sample size or comparison group are given, so `supported` rests only on a named, year-long applied study described in some detail. The measures (skin impedance at acupuncture points, quasi-stationary brain potential) are specialist and not standard practice. The text on PDF 461 refers the four groups to "(Fig 8.3)," but Fig 8.3 is the control-systems diagram on PDF 453; the restoration figure is Fig 8.4 on PDF 462. The text says Group II falls "between Groups I and III" while the group numbers suggest severity rises to IV; Group IV is illness, a different kind of state.

**Example** — The weekly sort as the authors give it: Group II gets local reflexive procedures on the problem zones plus a little general restoration; Group IV gets mainly general restoration under medical supervision (PDF 462 / p.451).

# Judge a Restoration Method by Performance and Injuries, Not Client Feeling, and Test It Under Sport-Typical Loads

**What it is** — Two rules for evaluating restoration. First: "Client feeling and appreciation are not enough; in sports restoration, the basic indicators are improved performance and fewer injuries." The reader should "experiment with variations, to keep records and to devise recipes which consistently yield successful results" (PDF 460 / p.449, checked against the page image). Second, from Talyshev (1977): because "it is very difficult to evaluate the effectiveness of specific recovery method," it "is more advisable to test the effectiveness of a specific recovery method by using test loads that approximate most closely the natural training conditions, by using loads in sports exercises that are typically encountered in a given sport" (PDF 460-461 / p.449-450, checked against the page images).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for caution: "if certain recovery methods are employed after a workout, then the positive after-effects (or training effect) stimulated by the workout tend to be negated," so "the unskilled use of recovery methods can markedly increase the amount of training work and yet not provide a corresponding training effect" (PDF 460 / p.449). Inference: an athlete can feel better and train more while adapting less, so feeling and session volume are the wrong outcome measures; performance and injury rate capture the net effect.

**When to apply** — When a modality is adopted or kept, write down what outcome it is meant to change, track performance and injuries across its use, and test it with the sport's own loads (for example a repeated-sprint or practice-like session) rather than a lab task. Eric's review: "Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89, Explicit). Inference: the same distrust of self-report that ended the surveys applies to "this feels good" as evidence for a recovery tool.

**When NOT to apply** — Performance and injury rate are slow, noisy outcomes; Inference: with a small group they cannot separate one modality's effect within a season, so the rule supports keeping records over time rather than quick verdicts. The book gives no example of a method that was dropped under this rule. Feeling still matters for adherence and is part of the placebo effect the authors elsewhere call useful (see [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]]).

**Example** — The authors' framing of Russian work: "systematic use of recovery methods makes it possible to significantly and sometimes rapidly increase the volume and intensity of training while simultaneously decreasing the incidence of musculoskeletal injuries" (PDF 460 / p.449), which names the two outcomes, training capacity and injuries, they want restoration judged on.
