# Three Classes of Restoration: Pedagogical (Coaching), Medico-Biological and Psychological, Plus Natural Recovery Outside Training

**What it is** — "The Russians usually recognise three classes of restoration (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 456 / p.445, checked against the page image):
- *Pedagogical (coaching) restoration* "employs carefully periodised programmes to optimise the balance between training stresses and natural recuperative processes." It includes "combinational training, known in the West as 'cross training'," active rest, and "Low intensity cyclical, rhythmical, circulatory or cardiovascular activities" after "demanding strength training sessions." Micro-, meso- and macrocycles, with the preparatory period split into General and Special Physical Preparation, exist "specifically to promote supercompensation via suitable phasing of loading and restoration regimes (see Ch 6)."
- *Medico-biological restoration* covers "therapeutic measures offered by medical and allied practitioners," sometimes split into physiotherapeutic and pharmacological measures. Physical measures divide into natural means ("massage, showers, heat, sunlight and training outdoors") and additional means ("electrostimulation, electrosleep, diathermy, acupuncture, baro-chambers, laser therapy and ultrasound").
- *Psychological restoration* "involves management of the mental state": hypnosis, self-hypnosis, auto-suggestion, autogenics, visualisation, progressive relaxation, guided imagery, music therapy and learning techniques, some using biofeedback or electrodermal devices.
Beyond these, "it is essential to encourage natural recovery relating to family, living conditions, lifestyle, nutrition, leisure activities, beneficial socialisation, team atmosphere, work conditions, spiritual needs and coaching team interaction" (PDF 456). A later restatement (PDF 458 / p.447, read from the page image) puts pedagogical methods "outside the scope of this text" and splits the rest into physical, medical and psychological means. Table 8.5 subdivides them: physical (passive, active, combined); medical (pharmacological, psychiatric, surgical, nutritional, combined); psychological (therapist-administered, self-administered, combined). Table 8.6 lists physical means in three columns, active means mainly in the last (for example physical activity, recreational sport, manual labour, dance, play, postural realignment, breathing regimens, progressive relaxation, Tai Chi, yoga); Table 8.7 lists 14 psychological means from psychotherapy to "Laughter/tears" (PDF 459 / p.448).

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale for the system is its specificity: "The Russian restoration system recognises the *specificity of each technique or sequence of techniques* for a particular sport, phase of training, individual athlete, time of the day, type of stress and type of fitness," applied "before, during, shortly after and a long time after training and competitions," with "Meticulous records" of daily physical and psychological state (PDF 456). On natural recovery: "problems which lie outside the training setting can easily predominate over training problems in determining the success of the athlete in competition" (PDF 456).

**When to apply** — As a coverage check on a recovery plan: is there a pedagogical element (load phasing, active rest), a medico-biological element (by whom), a psychological element, and attention to life outside training? The authors also note that "the athlete is encouraged to shed dependence on the therapist and to learn *self-restoration* procedures (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 456). Eric's review: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: by the book's scheme that is the pedagogical class only.

**When NOT to apply** — The categories are descriptive; the authors say Table 8.5 "should not be regarded as definitive or exclusive" (PDF 458). The lists mix well-studied means with ones that have little support (for example "Religion," "Screaming/shouting" in Table 8.7; "Therapeutic Touch," "Aromatherapy" in Table 8.6); inclusion is not endorsement of effect. Inference: the medico-biological class includes pharmacological means; anything in that class sits with the medical staff, not the strength coach.

**Example** — The pedagogical example the authors give: "Low intensity cyclical, rhythmical, circulatory or cardiovascular activities can also be very useful for promoting recovery after demanding strength training sessions" (PDF 456 / p.445).

**Related** — [[principle--restoration-is-part-of-training-and-distinct-from-rehabilitation]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]], [[framework--restoration-prescription-checklist-and-means-versus-methods]], [[framework--methods-for-improving-voluntary-muscle-relaxation]], [[browns-strength-and-conditioning-2008--myslinski/heuristic--restoration-emphasis-rises-as-the-off-season-advances]]

# Belief and Rapport Carry Much of a Restoration Technique's Effect, Which Is Both a Tool and a Confound

**What it is** — The authors: "Certainly, many of these techniques may work because they are placebos, because the user believes in them. Yet, this is a very good reason not to dismiss them." If the mind can be focused "by an apparently illogical or foolish concept to perform unusual feats of performance or healing, then it is vital that we uncover the underlying physiological principles which make the *placebo effect* (or 'faith factor') so powerful. Placebos can produce positive and negative effects; it is up to science to sift the useful from the harmful" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). The same effect "can also confound the validity of many restoration techniques, which work not because of any special merits, but because the practitioner persuades the user of its value." Hence "Virtually every claim by one massage therapist will be countered by another 'expert'" (PDF 455). On rapport: "the therapy often succeeds because of the rapport between therapist and client," and in sports restoration "*The rapport between you and the athlete is central to the success of the therapy*. In short, the belief of the athlete in you and your therapy (and sometimes an outside force, depending on the athlete's belief system) is an integral part of successful restoration" (PDF 456 / p.445, italics in the original, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "physical and mental healing are inextricably linked," so "one cannot separate the therapy from the therapist" (PDF 456). They draw the research consequence: "great care has to be taken to choose experimental and control groups and to exclude as far as possible all confounding factors such as the placebo effect and human interaction" (PDF 456). The 8.6 closing list makes the same point as propositions: "Virtually any technique will work, irrespective of scientific validity, if you believe in it," and a technique "obtained at high cost," taught "in an exciting, emotional or challenging way," or that "appeals to the basic beliefs, prejudices and background of the user is more likely to succeed" (items 1-4, PDF 467 / p.456).

**When to apply** — Two uses. Practice: before using any restoration means, "consider the background and attitudes of the athlete, because these factors can have a profound effect on the efficacy of any regime" (PDF 458 / p.447). Evaluation: when a staff member reports that a modality works, ask whether the comparison controlled for belief and attention. Inference: Eric's account of abandoned wellness surveys, where athletes learned what answers the survey rewarded (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89), is a reminder that self-report after a treatment carries the same bias.

**When NOT to apply** — These are the authors' opinions; no placebo-controlled data are given here. Two pages later the authors push the other way: "This [sic] is sometimes a tendency to dismiss the effects of many restorative means as placebo or psychological in origin," which their Russian research summary is meant "to correct" (PDF 465 / p.454; see [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]]). The two positions are not a contradiction in the book's own terms: belief adds to some real effects, and confounds the rest. Using belief deliberately raises an honesty question the book does not address.

**Example** — The authors' own contrast: "one therapist will swear that aromatherapy with a certain fragrance will help, while another may claim the opposite. Another will extol the virtue of deep transverse friction for adhesions, whereas yet another will have equal success with therapeutic touch" (PDF 455 / p.444).

**Related** — [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]], [[framework--eighteen-propositions-on-sport-science-and-stress-management]], [[heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]]

# What Stress Changes (Table 8.4), and Why Motor Control Belongs on the Monitoring List

**What it is** — Table 8.4, "Functions affected by physiological and psychological stress," introduced as "some of the symptoms of overtraining stress" (PDF 456 / p.445), lists 20 functions in three columns (PDF 457 / p.446, read from the page image): heart rate; blood pressure; muscular tension; muscle irritability; pain threshold; brain rhythms; breathing patterns; sleep patterns; body temperature; concentration and alertness; digestion, gastric acidity; endocrine secretion; immune response; fine motor control; reaction time; posture; pupil size (of the eye); general irritability, mood, stability; tissue repair and growth; secretion of endogenous opiates. The authors: "stress produces acute (short-term) and chronic (long-term) effects on variables including those listed in Table 8.4. There are many standard tests for and ways of observing most of the indicators of stress below; the thorough preparation of the athlete demands that they be applied regularly and appropriate restoration interventions be used" (PDF 457). Later they single out motor control: "careful attention has to be paid to changes in motor control or movement skill, since all sporting action relies fundamentally on muscle action controlled by the nervous system," which is why they earlier recommended "the coach making regular ratings of the technical perfection of the athlete's execution of important movements." "Quantitative measurement of individual indicators of motor proficiency, such as balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills, can also furnish useful data" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for motor control: it applies even to "training which does not necessarily place great demands on qualities such as strength and endurance" (PDF 461), because all sporting action runs through the nervous system. Inference: a technique or coordination drop can show stress in skill-dominant athletes before strength or endurance tests move.

**When to apply** — When choosing what to monitor, pick a few Table 8.4 functions that have a cheap test, and add one motor-control measure or a coach rating of technique. Eric's review: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: mRSI is a neuromuscular output measure; the book's list suggests reaction time or a coach technique rating as the complementary motor-control read.

**When NOT to apply** — The table is a list of functions, not a validated battery; it gives no tests, norms or thresholds, and "applied regularly" is not defined. Several items (brain rhythms, endogenous opiates, pupil size) need laboratory access. The authors' own text slips: it calls the table "symptoms of overtraining stress" and also functions affected by stress in general.

**Example** — The authors' motor-control battery: "balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills" (PDF 461 / p.450).

**What it is** — Table 8.4, "Functions affected by physiological and psychological stress," introduced as "some of the symptoms of overtraining stress" (PDF 456 / p.445), lists 20 functions in three columns (PDF 457 / p.446, read from the page image): heart rate; blood pressure; muscular tension; muscle irritability; pain threshold; brain rhythms; breathing patterns; sleep patterns; body temperature; concentration and alertness; digestion, gastric acidity; endocrine secretion; immune response; fine motor control; reaction time; posture; pupil size (of the eye); general irritability, mood, stability; tissue repair and growth; secretion of endogenous opiates. The authors: "stress produces acute (short-term) and chronic (long-term) effects on variables including those listed in Table 8.4. There are many standard tests for and ways of observing most of the indicators of stress below; the thorough preparation of the athlete demands that they be applied regularly and appropriate restoration interventions be used" (PDF 457). Later they single out motor control: "careful attention has to be paid to changes in motor control or movement skill, since all sporting action relies fundamentally on muscle action controlled by the nervous system," which is why they earlier recommended "the coach making regular ratings of the technical perfection of the athlete's execution of important movements" (the Ch 6.2 recommendation, see [[framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique]]). "Quantitative measurement of individual indicators of motor proficiency, such as balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills, can also furnish useful data" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for motor control: it applies even to "training which does not necessarily place great demands on qualities such as strength and endurance" (PDF 461), because all sporting action runs through the nervous system. Inference: a technique or coordination drop can show stress in skill-dominant athletes before strength or endurance tests move.

**When to apply** — When choosing what to monitor, pick a few Table 8.4 functions that have a cheap test, and add one motor-control measure or a coach rating of technique. Eric's review: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: mRSI is a neuromuscular output measure; the book's list suggests reaction time or a coach technique rating as the complementary motor-control read.

**When NOT to apply** — The table is a list of functions, not a validated battery; it gives no tests, norms or thresholds, and "applied regularly" is not defined. Several items (brain rhythms, endogenous opiates, pupil size) need laboratory access. The authors' own text slips: it calls the table "symptoms of overtraining stress" and also functions affected by stress in general.

**Example** — The authors' motor-control battery: "balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills" (PDF 461 / p.450).

# Makarova and Stupnitsky: Weekly Neuromuscular Screening Sorted Athletes Into Four Groups, Each With Its Own Restoration (Fig 8.4)

**What it is** — The authors describe a year-long applied system (Makarova & Stupnitsky, 1983). For athletes with access to scientific institutes, neuromuscular system (NMS) state "may be assessed by methods such as monitoring of the quasi-stationary electrical potential of the brain, quantitative muscle palpation (using probes such as the myotonometer devised by Siff) and measurement of skin conductance or impedance at acupuncture points (Shishkin, 1989)." Makarova & Stupnitsky found that local muscle contraction (LMC) measured by tonometry "displays a clear topography and often coincides with the acupuncture points," and that "pronounced LMC" coincided "with a poorer functional state of the NMS," together with "increased muscle tonus, decreased strength, an increase in time for muscle relaxation and impaired rheographic indicators" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image). Over year-long programmes they saw "a characteristic change in the skin impedance whenever there is significant disruption in the athlete's adaptation," and used it, "sometimes assisted by other standard physiological tests (such as heart rate, blood pressure, flicker fusion rate in vision and reaction time)," to adjust training and restoration (PDF 461). Athletes were sorted by these indicators and their self-perception: Group I, "no disruptions in self-feeling, work capacity or NMS"; Group II, "minor local disturbances"; Group III, "definite complaints and muscle disturbances"; Group IV, "acute illnesses (colds etc.)" (PDF 461). "This diagnostic process was repeated once per weekly microcycle." Restoration went mainly to Groups II-IV, "with minimal application to those in Group I." Group II received "point-reflexive and local reflexive procedures focusing on the problematic body zones," with "a small amount of general restoration"; in Group IV "general restoration means predominated over lesser used local reflexive methods," with the rehabilitative process "under medical supervision" (PDF 461-462 / p.450-451). Fig 8.4, "Organisation of the systems of restoration for athletes," read from the figure as far as its arrows can be traced (PDF 462 / p.451): Evaluation of the Functional State, linked to Consideration of Current Condition, feeds Groups I-IV; Groups II-IV feed Restorative Procedures, with an arrow from the groups to Therapeutic Procedures; Group I and Restorative Procedures feed the Training Process, which loops back to evaluation.

**Why it works** — The authors' account: these indicators "point to a diminished work capacity" (PDF 461), so they can direct restoration to the athletes who need it and leave the rest alone. Inference: it is a triage system; Group I athletes get almost no restoration, consistent with the book's warning that routine restoration can blunt adaptation.

**When to apply** — As a model for weekly triage: one screen per microcycle, a simple four-way sort (fine; local issue; general complaint; ill), and a different response for each, rather than one recovery routine for the roster.

**When NOT to apply** — The book reports the design, not the outcomes; no numbers, sample size or comparison group are given, so `supported` rests only on a named, year-long applied study described in some detail. The measures (skin impedance at acupuncture points, quasi-stationary brain potential) are specialist and not standard practice. The text on PDF 461 refers the four groups to "(Fig 8.3)," but Fig 8.3 is the control-systems diagram on PDF 453; the restoration figure is Fig 8.4 on PDF 462. The text says Group II falls "between Groups I and III" while the group numbers suggest severity rises to IV; Group IV is illness, a different kind of state.

**Example** — The weekly sort as the authors give it: Group II gets local reflexive procedures on the problem zones plus a little general restoration; Group IV gets mainly general restoration under medical supervision (PDF 462 / p.451).

# Judge a Restoration Method by Performance and Injuries, Not Client Feeling, and Test It Under Sport-Typical Loads

**What it is** — Two rules for evaluating restoration. First: "Client feeling and appreciation are not enough; in sports restoration, the basic indicators are improved performance and fewer injuries." The reader should "experiment with variations, to keep records and to devise recipes which consistently yield successful results" (PDF 460 / p.449, checked against the page image). Second, from Talyshev (1977): because "it is very difficult to evaluate the effectiveness of specific recovery method," it "is more advisable to test the effectiveness of a specific recovery method by using test loads that approximate most closely the natural training conditions, by using loads in sports exercises that are typically encountered in a given sport" (PDF 460-461 / p.449-450, checked against the page images).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for caution: "if certain recovery methods are employed after a workout, then the positive after-effects (or training effect) stimulated by the workout tend to be negated," so "the unskilled use of recovery methods can markedly increase the amount of training work and yet not provide a corresponding training effect" (PDF 460 / p.449). Inference: an athlete can feel better and train more while adapting less, so feeling and session volume are the wrong outcome measures; performance and injury rate capture the net effect.

**When to apply** — When a modality is adopted or kept, write down what outcome it is meant to change, track performance and injuries across its use, and test it with the sport's own loads (for example a repeated-sprint or practice-like session) rather than a lab task. Eric's review: "Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89, Explicit). Inference: the same distrust of self-report that ended the surveys applies to "this feels good" as evidence for a recovery tool.

**When NOT to apply** — Performance and injury rate are slow, noisy outcomes; Inference: with a small group they cannot separate one modality's effect within a season, so the rule supports keeping records over time rather than quick verdicts. The book gives no example of a method that was dropped under this rule. Feeling still matters for adherence and is part of the placebo effect the authors elsewhere call useful (see [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]]).

**Example** — The authors' framing of Russian work: "systematic use of recovery methods makes it possible to significantly and sometimes rapidly increase the volume and intensity of training while simultaneously decreasing the incidence of musculoskeletal injuries" (PDF 460 / p.449), which names the two outcomes, training capacity and injuries, they want restoration judged on.

**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]], [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]], [[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]]

Group II received "point-reflexive and local reflexive procedures focusing on the problematic body zones," with "a small amount of general restoration"; in Group IV "general restoration means predominated over lesser used local reflexive methods," with the rehabilitative process "under medical supervision" (PDF 461-462 / p.450-451). Fig 8.4, "Organisation of the systems of restoration for athletes," read from the figure as far as its arrows can be traced (PDF 462 / p.451): Evaluation of the Functional State, linked to Consideration of Current Condition, feeds Groups I-IV; Groups II-IV feed Restorative Procedures; Group IV also feeds Therapeutic Procedures, which return directly to evaluation; Group I and Restorative Procedures feed the Training Process, which loops back to evaluation. The direct Therapeutic route fits the text's "under medical supervision" for Group IV.

+**What it is** — The authors describe a year-long applied system (Makarova & Stupnitsky, 1983). For athletes with access to scientific institutes, neuromuscular system (NMS) state "may be assessed by methods such as monitoring of the quasi-stationary electrical potential of the brain, quantitative muscle palpation (using probes such as the myotonometer devised by Siff) and measurement of skin conductance or impedance at acupuncture points (Shishkin, 1989)." Makarova & Stupnitsky found that local muscle contraction (LMC) measured by tonometry "displays a clear topography and often coincides with the acupuncture points," and that "pronounced LMC" coincided "with a poorer functional state of the NMS," together with "increased muscle tonus, decreased strength, an increase in time for muscle relaxation and impaired rheographic indicators" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image). Over year-long programmes they saw "a characteristic change in the skin impedance whenever there is significant disruption in the athlete's adaptation," and used it, "sometimes assisted by other standard physiological tests (such as heart rate, blood pressure, flicker fusion rate in vision and reaction time)," to adjust training and restoration (PDF 461). Athletes were sorted by these indicators and their self-perception: Group I, "no disruptions in self-feeling, work capacity or NMS"; Group II, "minor local disturbances"; Group III, "definite complaints and muscle disturbances"; Group IV, "acute illnesses (colds etc.)" (PDF 461). "This diagnostic process was repeated once per weekly microcycle." Restoration went mainly to Groups II-IV, "with minimal application to those in Group I." Group II received "point-reflexive and local reflexive procedures focusing on the problematic body zones," with "a small amount of general restoration"; in Group IV "general restoration means predominated over lesser used local reflexive methods," with the rehabilitative process "under medical supervision" (PDF 461-462 / p.450-451). Fig 8.4, "Organisation of the systems of restoration for athletes," read from the figure as far as its arrows can be traced (PDF 462 / p.451): Evaluation of the Functional State, linked to Consideration of Current Condition, feeds Groups I-IV; Groups II-IV feed Restorative Procedures; Group IV also feeds Therapeutic Procedures, which return directly to evaluation; Group I and Restorative Procedures feed the Training Process, which loops back to evaluation. Inference: the direct Therapeutic route fits the text's "under medical supervision" for Group IV.

**Why it works** — The authors' account: these indicators "point to a diminished work capacity" (PDF 461), so they can direct restoration to the athletes who need it and leave the rest alone. Inference: it is a triage system; Group I athletes get almost no restoration, consistent with the book's warning that routine restoration can blunt adaptation.

28:**When NOT to apply** — "Successfully" is the book's word; no performance or injury data are given, so `untested`. The programme is for elite track cyclists with full-time medical and therapy staff; many means (ionised air, light therapy, barometric techniques) are not available or supported in most programmes. Inference: the AM/PM pattern assumes two sessions a day; a one-session team day cannot copy it directly. The Day 4 PM cell is blank in the table, with no explanation.
26:**When NOT to apply** — The tables are lists without evidence of effect for each method; inclusion of Therapeutic Touch and barotherapy is not support for them. The contraindication list "refers specifically to massage which makes definite contact with the body" and "only to physical contra-indications; there are also several good psychological or ethical reasons why massage might be contraindicated" (PDF 460). Some entries reflect the book's era and are not current clinical guidance as written (for example, the menstruation item). Inference: in a university setting, contraindication screening sits with licensed medical staff.
19:3. "Massage generally has a favourable influence on all subsystems of the body, optimising their state by increasing or decreasing the level of activation of the cortex and sub-cortical systems of the brain."
23:**Why it works** — The authors' reading (finding 3) is that massage "optimises" state rather than pushing it one way. Inference, from the figure: in most panels the "max" line falls and the "min" line rises, so groups converge toward the middle; for example skin resistance and reaction time fall in the max group and rise in the min group under all four techniques. The figure is not uniform: under stroking, tonometer readings fall in all three groups and dynamometer force stays roughly flat (max, mean) or falls (min), while under squeezing, kneading and percussion both indices rise in all three groups.
9:confidence: supported
16:**What it is** — Two Russian findings the authors cite. Dubrovsky (1982), using "the injection of radioactive Xenon markers into the blood," found that "sports massage dilates the peripheral blood vessels, speeds up venous and muscle blood flow, and causes a small, but significant, increase in the oxygen saturation of arterial blood"; concurrent myotonometer readings "revealed a decrease in muscle tone," which Dubrovsky attributed to the enhanced blood flow (PDF 465 / p.454, checked against the page image). Burovykh et al (1976): "mechanical vibromassage (35-100 Hz) causes an acute decrease in blood circulation, associated with the vasoconstrictive effect of vibration," and "the increase in muscle blood supply after manual massage is due primarily to dilation of the lumen of the small arterial vessels, rather than the popularly believed concept of venous drainage." The same work linked blood-flow gains to "the tissue warming effects of some forms of massage" and showed "a decrease in muscle temperature (0.5-1.0 deg C) due to vibromassage" (PDF 465, numbers checked against the page image).
18:**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: manual massage dilates small arteries and warms tissue; high-frequency vibration constricts vessels and cools muscle (PDF 465). The authors' implication: "deep manual massage is more effective for enhancing blood flow and relaxation than higher frequency vibromassage, which should be used for the reflexogenic application of stimulating the neuromuscular system." With an adjustable vibromassager, "lower frequencies (10-15 Hz) can be used to promote general restoration, blood flow, muscle relaxation and decreased arterial pressure, provided that care is taken not to apply it over nervous plexuses or prominent bony areas" (PDF 465). They add that Dubrovsky's tone finding "emphasizes that mild active restoration offers some definite advantages over strictly passive methods on their own" (PDF 465).
22:**When NOT to apply** — The studies are cited, not described: no sample sizes, protocols or effect sizes beyond the 0.5-1.0 deg C temperature drop and the frequency bands. The 35-100 Hz finding is for 1970s mechanical vibromassagers; Inference: modern percussion devices differ in amplitude and contact, so the result transfers only by analogy. The 10-15 Hz recommendation is the authors' inference from these studies, not a tested protocol. The Dubrovsky sentence is printed ungrammatically ("conclude that decrease in muscle tone caused by enhanced blood flow"), so the direction of cause is the reading most consistent with the context.
24:**Example** — Burovykh et al's contrast: manual massage raised muscle blood supply through arterial dilation, while vibromassage at 35-100 Hz cut circulation and lowered muscle temperature by 0.5-1.0 deg C (PDF 465 / p.454).
27:**When NOT to apply** — The list cites no studies; items 7 and 16-18 (the "superconscious," Jung's types, a "seldom-tapped source of energy") are speculative and outside sport science as practised. Item 1 ("any technique will work ... if you believe in it") overstates the placebo point the authors make more carefully on PDF 455-456, and item 9 qualifies item 8 on the same page. Treat the list as the authors' views, not findings.

# Soviet Track Cycling: Three Groups of Restorative Means Matched to Each Training Stage, and a Shock Microcycle With Restoration Twice a Day (Table 8.11)

**What it is** — "The Soviet track cycling team, for a period of 5 years, successfully used this type of programme of restoration, (Goletz & Osadchy, 1986)," with three groups of means: "Group 1 (Basic means) for rapidly eliminating the fatigue following a training session"; "Group 2 (On-going means) for restoring the individual components of athletic preparedness to elevate the work capacity of these components during subsequent training sessions"; "Group 3 (Operative means) for stimulating work capacity directly before or during a workout or competition" (PDF 463 / p.452, checked against the page image). By stage:
- *General base-building*: "only *basic* type restorative means," because the stage has "concentrated, high-volume workloads." At the end of the microcycle, before a rest day: a hydro session or short gentle swim, restorative massage, warm baths with essences (pine, eucalyptus, sea salt), and a hot-cold contrast bath or shower (PDF 463).
- *Progressing training*: basic and on-going means per the microcycle plan, adding localised manual massage, showers and light therapy; at microcycle end, hydro procedures with electrotherapy, electromagnetic fields, ultrasound and barometric techniques (PDF 463).
- *Winter indoor competitions*: more "non-relaxing *operative* means." Sprint and heat groups: "brisk pre-start massage of the primary working leg muscles ... for 8-12 minutes; massage of the segmental areas of the back and torso for 3-5 minutes." Pace groups: hot pine-bath hydromassage "for 3-5 minutes, needle or cold shower for 8-13 minutes," and brisk pre-start leg massage "for 8-12 minutes" among other steps (PDF 463, numbers checked against the page image).
- *Outdoor track competitions*: "15-20 minutes before," brisk massage "for 8-10 minutes" with heating embrocations; after, "a warm pine or sea bath for 10-15 minutes, a warm rain-type shower and restorative massage for 30 minutes" (PDF 464 / p.453, checked against the page image).
- *Immediate pre-competitive preparation* is "The most concentrated period of use of physical means," with "the entire arsenal," including progressive relaxation, self-hypnosis, guided imagery and autogenics (PDF 464).
Table 8.11 gives a pre-competition "'shock' microcycle," read cell by cell from the page image (PDF 464 / p.453), as type/magnitude then restorative measures. AM: Day 1 aerobic/medium, warm salt bath; Day 2 aerobic/medium, localised hand massage; Day 3 aerobic/light, contrast rain-type shower and segmental massage; Day 4 aerobic/light, sauna and local hand massage; Day 5 aerobic/medium, localised hand massage; Day 6 aerobic/medium, warm salt bath; Day 7 aerobic/medium, contrast rain-type shower and segmental massage. PM: Day 1 anaerobic/medium, warm pine bath and local hand massage with restorative balsams; Day 2 speed/heavy, indifferent equivalent bath, hydromassage, warm rain shower; Day 3 anaerobic/heavy, hot pine bath, Charcot shower (stream), local massage of the working muscles with restorative balsams; Day 4 blank; Day 5 complex/heavy, warm pine bath, hydromassage, warm rain-type shower; Day 6 complex/medium, warm equivalent bath, hot stream shower, local massage of working muscles; Day 7 complex/heavy, sauna, whole-body restorative massage, contrast procedures.

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale: "Because the same restorative means diminish their effectiveness when they are used over prolonged periods, the restorative means were alternated, regarding both content and volume, depending on the stage of the annual cycle" (PDF 463). Throughout, "Special local muscle relaxing and range of movement activities formed an integral component of all training sessions to minimise drops in training effectiveness due to negative acute after-effects of any exercises" (PDF 464). Inference: the table pairs the heaviest restoration (sauna and whole-body massage, hot pine bath with Charcot shower) with the heavy PM sessions and keeps the AM aerobic sessions on light means.

**When to apply** — As a template for writing restoration into a periodised plan: basic means in high-volume base stages, on-going means as specialisation rises, operative (stimulating) means before competition, and a day-by-day restorative column in the microcycle table.

**When NOT to apply** — "Successfully" is the book's word; no performance or injury data are given, so `untested`. The programme is for elite track cyclists with full-time medical and therapy staff; many means (ionised air, light therapy, barometric techniques) are not available or supported in most programmes. Inference: the AM/PM pattern assumes two sessions a day; a one-session team day cannot copy it directly. The Day 4 PM cell is blank in the table, with no explanation.

**Example** — Day 3 of the shock microcycle: an AM aerobic/light session with a contrast rain-type shower and segmental massage, then a PM anaerobic/heavy session followed by a hot pine bath, Charcot shower and local massage of the working muscles with restorative balsams (Table 8.11, PDF 464 / p.453).

**Related** — [[principle--periodise-restoration-in-complexes-not-at-random]], [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]], [[heuristic--shock-microcycle-limits]], [[framework--matveyev-microcycle-and-mesocycle-types-and-sequences]], [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]]

# Massage as a Prescribed Means: Its Methods, Variables, Sport Roles and Contraindications (Tables 8.8-8.10)

**What it is** — "The popularity of massage deems that further details of its different methods be given" (PDF 459 / p.448). From the page images:
- *Methods* (Table 8.8, PDF 459 / p.448), 20 cells in two columns: effleurage (long, smooth stroking); frottage (rubbing); petrissage (kneading); friction (deep kneading); tapotement (percussion); vibration (trembling, shaking); nerve stroking (light stroking); "Rolling, wringing, jostling"; squeezing; drilling; pressing (sustained or oscillatory); slapping; hacking; "Lifting, pulling"; "Clapping, cupping"; deep transverse friction; Therapeutic Touch; cryokinetics; barotherapy; electrostimulation.
- *Variables* (Table 8.9, PDF 459), 20: means, methods, apparatus, hand or other massaging contact, depth, frequency, pressure, lubricant, positioning, sequence; duration, tempo, environment, psychological state, direction, rest intervals, therapist personal features, client personal features, variation, "Ethics, privacy, respect." The text adds contact points (palms, finger tips, knuckles, knife-edge of hand, thumb, fist, elbow, feet) and modes of movement (linear, circular, spiral, transverse or longitudinal to the muscle, pulsating, vibrating, squeezing, twisting, pinching, lifting, pressing).
- *Roles in sports preparation*, "as described by many Russian experts": "Warming; Loosening; Pre-start relaxation; Pre-start stimulation; Mobilisation; Restoration during and after workouts or competitions" (PDF 459-460 / p.448-449).
- *Contraindications* (Table 8.10, PDF 460 / p.449), 18: broken or bleeding tissue; inflamed, bruised, swollen tissue; strains, sprains, tissue rupture; varicose veins; painful, hypersensitive regions; phlebitis; thrombosis; swellings, lumps, moles, warts; fractures; arthritis with inflammation; stomach area during pregnancy; stomach area during nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, gastric upset; haemorrhaged tissue; jaundice; "Thigh, hip, chest, gluteal massage during menstruation"; dermatitis, urticaria or any skin irritation or allergy; contagious conditions; malignant tissue.

**Why it works** — The authors treat massage "like any other form of therapy," which "can pose certain risks" (PDF 460). Inference: separating method (what is done) from variables (how it is dosed) and role (why) is what lets two sessions called "massage" be compared at all; without it, the claims and counter-claims the authors describe cannot be tested.

**When to apply** — When a massage is part of a warm-up, a pre-start routine or restoration, state its role first (warming, loosening, relaxing, stimulating, mobilising, restoring), then pick method and variables to fit, then screen against the contraindications. The authors also require the practitioner to "be aware of any personal limitations" and call on someone "more qualified in certain fields" (PDF 460).

**When NOT to apply** — The tables are lists without evidence of effect for each method; inclusion of Therapeutic Touch and barotherapy is not support for them. The contraindication list "refers specifically to massage which makes definite contact with the body" and "only to physical contra-indications; there are also several good psychological or ethical reasons why massage might be contraindicated" (PDF 460). Some entries reflect the book's era and are not current clinical guidance as written (for example, the menstruation item). Inference: in a university setting, contraindication screening sits with licensed medical staff.

**Example** — The six roles applied to a pre-race routine in the book's own cycling case: "brisk pre-start massage of the primary working leg muscles (using stroking, rubbing, kneading, shaking) for 8-12 minutes" is the "pre-start stimulation" role (PDF 463 / p.452; see [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]]).

**Related** — [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]], [[claim--manual-massage-raises-blood-flow-while-high-frequency-vibromassage-lowers-it]], [[heuristic--choose-massage-technique-by-goal]], [[framework--restoration-prescription-checklist-and-means-versus-methods]], [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]] (the complementarity effect)

# Massage Effects Depend on the Athlete's Initial State and the Technique Used, Not Only Placebo (Birukov and Pelsahov, Fig 8.5)

**What it is** — To "correct" the "tendency to dismiss the effects of many restorative means as placebo or psychological in origin," the authors cite Birukov & Pelsahov (1979), who found that massage "indeed causes effects which are not simply placebo or circulatory in nature," with "different effects of massage on the central and peripheral systems, as well as differences in the effects produced by each different type of massage (Fig 8.5)" (PDF 465 / p.454, checked against the page image). Four findings:
1. "Massage does not have an identical effect on the central and peripheral systems of the body. The condition of the peripheral systems changes in the same direction, while the functional state of the brain changes over a much wider range, depending on the initial levels existing before the massage."
2. "Individual massage methods change the condition of the separate subsystems of the body in different ways. The influence of individual massage techniques depends largely on the initial functional condition before the application of massage."
3. "Massage generally has a favourable influence on all subsystems of the body, optimising their state by increasing or decreasing the level of activation of the cortex and sub-cortical systems of the brain."
4. "When using massage as a method of restructuring and restoring, it is necessary to differentiate the approach by taking into consideration the initial level of excitation," using measures "such as simple reaction time, skin impedance, dynamometry and tonometry" (PDF 465).
Fig 8.5 (PDF 466 / p.455, read from the figure) plots four indices (reaction time, axis about 149-157; skin resistance in kilo-ohm, about 30-110; dynamometer force in kgf, about 40-60; tonometer reading in mm, about 70-90) before and after four techniques (stroking; squeezing; kneading; slapping, clapping, percussion), with three lines each: athletes with maximum, mean and minimum initial values. The caption calls these "three groups of athletes, distinguished by their initial levels."

**Why it works** — The authors' reading (finding 3) is that massage "optimises" state rather than pushing it one way. Inference, from the figure: in most panels the "max" line falls and the "min" line rises, so groups converge toward the middle; for example skin resistance and reaction time fall in the max group and rise in the min group under all four techniques. The figure is not uniform: under stroking, tonometer readings fall in all three groups and dynamometer force stays roughly flat (max, mean) or falls (min), while under squeezing, kneading and percussion both indices rise in all three groups.

**When to apply** — Before choosing a massage technique for restoration, measure or at least judge the athlete's starting state (aroused or flat), since the same technique can move different athletes in different directions. The authors' indicators are reaction time, skin impedance, grip dynamometry and tonometry (PDF 465).

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample size, statistics or control condition, and the figure's reaction-time axis has no unit. The convergence pattern is this entry's reading of the figure, not a statement in the text. Inference: grouping athletes by their extreme initial values invites regression to the mean, which would make max groups fall and min groups rise even without any treatment; the book does not address this.

**Example** — Finding 4 in practice: the authors tie the choice of massage approach to "the initial level of excitation," measured by "simple reaction time, skin impedance, dynamometry and tonometry" (PDF 465 / p.454).

# Manual Massage Raises Muscle Blood Flow by Dilating Small Arteries; Mechanical Vibromassage at 35-100 Hz Lowers It

**What it is** — Two Russian findings the authors cite. Dubrovsky (1982), using "the injection of radioactive Xenon markers into the blood," found that "sports massage dilates the peripheral blood vessels, speeds up venous and muscle blood flow, and causes a small, but significant, increase in the oxygen saturation of arterial blood"; concurrent myotonometer readings "revealed a decrease in muscle tone," which Dubrovsky attributed to the enhanced blood flow (PDF 465 / p.454, checked against the page image). Burovykh et al (1976): "mechanical vibromassage (35-100 Hz) causes an acute decrease in blood circulation, associated with the vasoconstrictive effect of vibration," and "the increase in muscle blood supply after manual massage is due primarily to dilation of the lumen of the small arterial vessels, rather than the popularly believed concept of venous drainage." The same work linked blood-flow gains to "the tissue warming effects of some forms of massage" and showed "a decrease in muscle temperature (0.5-1.0 deg C) due to vibromassage" (PDF 465, numbers checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: manual massage dilates small arteries and warms tissue; high-frequency vibration constricts vessels and cools muscle (PDF 465). The authors' implication: "deep manual massage is more effective for enhancing blood flow and relaxation than higher frequency vibromassage, which should be used for the reflexogenic application of stimulating the neuromuscular system." With an adjustable vibromassager, "lower frequencies (10-15 Hz) can be used to promote general restoration, blood flow, muscle relaxation and decreased arterial pressure, provided that care is taken not to apply it over nervous plexuses or prominent bony areas" (PDF 465). They add that Dubrovsky's tone finding "emphasizes that mild active restoration offers some definite advantages over strictly passive methods on their own" (PDF 465).

**When to apply** — When a percussion or vibration device is used for "recovery," check its frequency and the aim: for blood flow and relaxation, the book favours deep manual work or low-frequency (10-15 Hz) vibration; for stimulation before effort, higher-frequency vibration. Eric's review: "recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: by these findings a high-frequency percussion gun is a stimulation tool more than a blood-flow tool.

**When NOT to apply** — The studies are cited, not described: no sample sizes, protocols or effect sizes beyond the 0.5-1.0 deg C temperature drop and the frequency bands. The 35-100 Hz finding is for 1970s mechanical vibromassagers; Inference: modern percussion devices differ in amplitude and contact, so the result transfers only by analogy. The 10-15 Hz recommendation is the authors' inference from these studies, not a tested protocol. The Dubrovsky sentence is printed ungrammatically ("conclude that decrease in muscle tone caused by enhanced blood flow"), so the direction of cause is the reading most consistent with the context.

**Example** — Burovykh et al's contrast: manual massage raised muscle blood supply through arterial dilation, while vibromassage at 35-100 Hz cut circulation and lowered muscle temperature by 0.5-1.0 deg C (PDF 465 / p.454).

**Related** — [[heuristic--choose-massage-technique-by-goal]], [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (low-frequency vibromassage in runners), [[research-papers/dupuy-2018-an-evidence-based-approach-for-choosing-post-exercise-recovery-techniques-to-reduce-marker]]

# Eighteen Propositions on Sport Science and Stress Management

**What it is** — The last sub-section of 8.6, "Sports Science and Stress Management," sits at the top of PDF 467 / p.456, above the 8.7 heading. The authors: "all training is a form of stressing the body in an optimal manner," and training principles "are very useful in helping one cope with physical and mental stress both in and away from the competitive arena." They then give a list "assembled largely from previous chapters of this text" (PDF 467, checked against the page image). Grouped here by theme (the grouping is this entry's; numbers are the book's):
- *Belief and delivery* (1-4): "Virtually any technique will work, irrespective of scientific validity, if you believe in it"; techniques obtained "at high cost in terms of effort, cash or commitment," taught "in an exciting, emotional or challenging way," or appealing to "the basic beliefs, prejudices and background of the user" are more likely to succeed.
- *Individual and dynamic* (5-6, 14): "No technique is universally superior to another: a given technique is better for a given individual in a given situation at a given time"; stress "is not static, but a dynamic physiological and psychological process"; it "may be managed by use of physiological or psychological techniques."
- *Dose and adaptation* (8-12): optimise, "though not necessarily avoid or diminish stress"; but "The concept of stress optimisation is not always accurate: high performance may occur with altered states of consciousness when stress levels are very high or very low"; exposure "may produce either adaptation or sensitisation"; the first response may be "flight or fight, but also freezing ... which may be the most damaging effect of stress"; planned exposure to manageable stress "may enable one to cope with higher levels of stress."
- *Perception and movement* (13, 15): understanding "kinaesthetic and motor" processes "is invaluable"; "Our perception or interpretation of stress or pain may be more powerful than the stress, pain or stimulus itself."
- *Mind models* (7, 16-18): the subconscious or "superconscious"; Jung's four functions (sensation, intuition, thinking, feeling); brain regions beyond the left-right cortex; and access to "a vast seldom-tapped source of energy via specific altered states of consciousness."

**Why it works** — The authors' frame is that stress tolerance is trainable like any other quality: "*Superadaptation* (supercompensation) or *innoculation* against specific stresses is possible by exposing yourself to properly structured doses of manageable stress" (PDF 467). Inference: items 8-12 carry the training logic; items 1-4 and 15 carry the psychological logic that the placebo discussion earlier in 8.6 develops.

**When to apply** — As a set of prompts when an athlete's response to stress (competition, injury, life events) is the problem: is the response adaptation or sensitisation (10), freezing rather than fight-or-flight (11), driven by perception more than the stressor (15)? Inference: items 5 and 10 argue for individual, revised plans rather than a fixed team routine.

**When NOT to apply** — The list cites no studies; items 7 and 16-18 (the "superconscious," Jung's types, a "seldom-tapped source of energy") are speculative and outside sport science as practised. Item 1 ("any technique will work ... if you believe in it") overstates the placebo point the authors make more carefully on PDF 455-456, and item 9 qualifies item 8 on the same page. Treat the list as the authors' views, not findings.

**Example** — Item 15 in the authors' own words: "alteration of our perceptions and thoughts may manage the stress effectively," and "our perception or assessment of the attractiveness or repulsiveness of the stressor can alter our belief that the stressor can be managed" (PDF 467 / p.456).

- Fixer: Claude Opus 5.5 (fixer pass)
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Review file: `staging/review_supertraining_ch8b_opus.md` (verdict GO AFTER FIXES, required fixes 1-15)
- Folder: `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`

- Not touched: vault, `_book.md` (no fix needed a row change), cross-linked files on scope lines 32-37 (no fix named them).

| File | Change made | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| framework--matveyev-categorisation-of-competitive-exercises-table-8-2.md | "When to apply": "As a first sort ... borrow programming from neighbours" now opens "Inference:" | 1 |
| framework--medvedev-weightlifting-exercise-groups-fundamental-and-additional-means.md | "When to apply": removed "single-joint assistance work would be additional"; now says most of Eric's multi-joint assistance lifts (lunges, rows, seated and incline presses) would be additional, his single-joint work has no named place, and the book's line is technique conformity and power output, not joint count, listing groups 13-16 (PDF 446 / p.435) | 2 |
| heuristic--calculate-fundamental-and-additional-training-loads-separately.md | "When to apply": Inference reworded so the split is heavy, high-power, competition-pattern lifts versus lighter, local, technique-different work, not multi-joint versus single-joint | 3 |
| heuristic--calculate-fundamental-and-additional-training-loads-separately.md | "Example": "lunges, good mornings and presses" changed to "lunges, hyperextensions and seated or incline presses" (only additional items, groups 13-15) | 3 |
| framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3.md | "When NOT to apply": added the Morris link and the difference (Morris ties addisonic to too much volume and basedowic to too much intensity; Table 8.3 gives symptoms, not causes; not a conflict). Added the same link to "Related" | 4 |
| principle--restoration-is-part-of-training-and-distinct-from-rehabilitation.md | "When to apply": "have no counterpart in the baseline" changed to "have only a secondary place in the baseline (line 151 ...)", with the line-151 quote | 5 |
| framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological.md | "What it is": Table 8.6 now has its own locator, PDF 458 / p.447. Table 8.7 keeps PDF 459 | 6 |
| framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological.md | "When to apply": "pedagogical class only" changed to "mainly the pedagogical class", with line 151 cited (recovery technology as a secondary medico-biological means) | 6 |
| framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological.md | "When NOT to apply": "The lists mix well-studied means ..." now opens "Inference:" | 6 |
| claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect.md | "When NOT to apply": "Two pages later" changed to "Later in 8.6, under Research into Restoration Methods," | 7 |
| framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring.md | "What it is": link to `framework--cybernetic-periodisation-rpe-and-rating-of-technique` added after the "earlier recommended" quote. Added the same link to "Related" | 8 |
| case-study--makarova-stupnitsky-weekly-four-group-restoration-triage-fig-8-4.md | "What it is": Fig 8.4 reading rewritten: Group IV also feeds Therapeutic Procedures, which go straight back to evaluation. Added an "Inference:" sentence: this fits "under medical supervision" | 9 |
| heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads.md | "When to apply": the baseline line-89 quote now includes the qualifier about return-to-play and chronic conditions. The Inference now says Eric does not reject self-report outright | 10 |
| case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11.md | "When NOT to apply": the "many means ... not available or supported" clause is now its own sentence opening "Inference:" | 11 |
| framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications.md | "When NOT to apply": "Some entries reflect the book's era ..." now opens "Inference:" | 12 |
| claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5.md | "Why it works": "in most panels" changed to "in the reaction-time and skin-resistance rows (8 of 16 panels)". Added "Inference: so the finding-3 "optimising" reading rests on half the figure." | 13 |
| claim--manual-massage-raises-blood-flow-while-high-frequency-vibromassage-lowers-it.md | Frontmatter `confidence: supported` changed to `untested` (the review's first option) | 14 |
| framework--eighteen-propositions-on-sport-science-and-stress-management.md | "When NOT to apply": the items 7 and 16-18 judgment and the item 1 judgment now each open "Inference:" | 15 |

Files changed: 15. Fixes applied in full: 15 of 15.

## Fix 14: which option was taken

I lowered the confidence to `untested` rather than keeping `supported` and narrowing it to Dubrovsky. The entry's title and Example rest on the vibromassage half, which comes from Burovykh et al, and the book does not describe that study. I left the sentence "The studies are cited, not described" unchanged, as the first option allows. A later pass could note that Dubrovsky's method is partly described (radioactive Xenon markers, myotonometry).

## Not applied: missing ideas 1-5, carried to coverage follow-up

The brief says not to add these. They are carried forward for a coverage follow-up:

1. Zalessky's three phases of normal recovery: on-going, rapid and delayed (PDF 455 / p.444).
2. Deeper workout fatigue gives larger after-effects when loads are prescribed carefully. Talyshev's two sides of recovery: immediate, as in competition, versus recovery in daily training (PDF 460 / p.449).
3. Goal-directed episodes of inaction. Western athletes copy the sessions but ignore what happens between them (PDF 455 / p.444).
4. "Individualisation of approach is vital, as is variation, though not simply for the sake of it" (PDF 455).
5. The practitioner Code of Conduct and the duty to refer to someone more qualified (PDF 460). The massage entry only touches this.

## Optional items (not blocking, not applied)

- Name 1.15.3 as the misprint in `claim--overtraining-is-accumulated...` and in the fitness-fatigue Also-in line.
- The title of `framework--bench-squat-and-deadlift-variation-axes.md` lists six axes, but the body has seven (instability).

## Fixes not applied exactly as written

None. Fix 2 gave example wording ("e.g."). I kept its substance and named the presses as seated and incline, because standing press and push-press are fundamental group 12 (PDF 446).

## Lint

`FLINT_VAULT=/Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain python3 scripts/lint_library.py strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky` reported TOTAL ISSUES: 0. That covers the 15 changed files and the whole folder. The review counted 3 em-dash hits in `_book.md`; this run reported none, and `_book.md` was not edited.
